claim: In Marvel Comics, Peter Parker gains his powers after being bitten by a radioactive spider.
explanation: Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962) establishes that a radioactive spider bite gives Peter Parker his powers.

claim: In the MCU film Iron Man (2008), Tony Stark is captured by terrorists in Vietnam.
explanation: In the 2008 film Stark is captured in Afghanistan by the Ten Rings. Vietnam is the setting of the original 1963 comic origin.

claim: In the MCU, Steve Rogers becomes Captain America after receiving the Super-Soldier Serum.
explanation: In Captain America: The First Avenger, Dr. Abraham Erskine's serum transforms the frail Steve Rogers into a super-soldier.
source_name: Wikipedia - Captain America: The First Avenger

claim: In Marvel Comics, Thor's hammer Mjolnir is made of vibranium.
explanation: In the comics Mjolnir is forged from uru metal and enchanted by Odin. Vibranium is the metal of Wakanda.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Bruce Banner becomes the Hulk after exposure to gamma radiation.
explanation: The Incredible Hulk #1 (1962) shows Banner caught in the blast of a gamma bomb, which causes his transformations.

claim: In Marvel Comics, the Hulk was green in his very first issue, The Incredible Hulk #1 (1962).
explanation: The Hulk was gray in The Incredible Hulk #1; he was changed to green starting with issue #2 because of printing problems with the gray coloring.

claim: In the MCU, King T'Chaka of Wakanda is killed in a bombing at a United Nations conference in Vienna in Captain America: Civil War.
explanation: The Vienna bombing, orchestrated by Helmut Zemo, kills T'Chaka and sets T'Challa on a path of vengeance in Civil War.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Black Panther's suit is woven with adamantium.
explanation: The Black Panther suit is made with vibranium, Wakanda's signature metal. Adamantium is associated with Wolverine and Captain America-era alloys.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Stephen Strange is a renowned neurosurgeon before he becomes a sorcerer.
explanation: Doctor Strange's origin has him as a brilliant but arrogant surgeon whose hands are ruined in a car accident, leading him to the mystic arts.

claim: In the MCU film Doctor Strange (2016), Stephen Strange travels to Tokyo to find Kamar-Taj.
explanation: In the film Strange travels to Kathmandu, Nepal, where he finds Kamar-Taj.

claim: In the MCU, Natasha Romanoff was trained as an assassin in the Red Room program.
explanation: The MCU establishes the Red Room as the Soviet-linked program that trained Natasha Romanoff, most fully depicted in Black Widow (2021).

claim: In the MCU, Natasha Romanoff sacrifices herself on Vormir to obtain the Mind Stone.
explanation: In Avengers: Endgame her sacrifice on Vormir obtains the Soul Stone. The Mind Stone was already in Vision's head in this timeline.

claim: In the MCU film Ant-Man (2015), Hank Pym recruits Scott Lang to become the new Ant-Man.
explanation: Hank Pym selects ex-convict Scott Lang to wear the Ant-Man suit and carry out a heist against Darren Cross.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Hope van Dyne was the first character to use the name the Wasp.
explanation: Janet van Dyne was the original Wasp, debuting in Tales to Astonish #44 (1963).

claim: In Marvel Comics, Carol Danvers gains her powers after an explosion of a Kree device called the Psyche-Magnetron.
explanation: Her comics origin has the Psyche-Magnetron explosion fusing Kree DNA with hers, giving her superhuman abilities.

claim: In the MCU film Captain Marvel (2019), Carol Danvers gains her powers from the Power Stone.
explanation: In the film she is exposed to energy from the Tesseract, which contains the Space Stone, when an engine is destroyed.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Matt Murdock loses his sight in a childhood accident involving a radioactive substance.
explanation: As a boy Matt is blinded by radioactive material while saving a man, which also heightens his other senses.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Matt Murdock's father Jack Murdock was a firefighter.
explanation: Jack Murdock was a boxer, not a firefighter.

claim: In Marvel Comics, the Fantastic Four gain their powers from exposure to cosmic rays during an unauthorized space flight.
explanation: Fantastic Four #1 (1961) shows Reed Richards, Sue Storm, Johnny Storm and Ben Grimm bombarded by cosmic rays in space.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Sue Storm's powers include control of fire.
explanation: Sue Storm is the Invisible Woman, with invisibility and force fields. Her brother Johnny Storm controls fire.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Ben Grimm, the future Thing, was the pilot of the rocket in the Fantastic Four's origin.
explanation: Ben Grimm is a former test pilot who flies the unauthorized flight on which the team is exposed to cosmic rays.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Doctor Doom is the ruler of Wakanda.
explanation: Doctor Doom rules the fictional Eastern European nation of Latveria. Wakanda is ruled by the Black Panther.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Charles Xavier founds the X-Men.
explanation: Professor Charles Xavier assembles the original X-Men in The X-Men #1 (1963) to train young mutants.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Storm's mutant power is the ability to control magnetism.
explanation: Storm controls the weather. Magnetism is Magneto's power.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Scott Summers (Cyclops) has a younger brother, Alex Summers, who is known as Havok.
explanation: Alex Summers is Scott's younger brother and uses the codename Havok.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Kitty Pryde's mutant power is teleportation.
explanation: Kitty Pryde can phase through solid matter. Nightcrawler is the X-Man who teleports.

claim: In the MCU, Peter Quill is abducted from Earth as a child in 1988.
explanation: Guardians of the Galaxy opens in 1988 with young Peter Quill taken by the Ravagers after his mother's death.

claim: In the MCU, Gamora's adoptive father is Ronan the Accuser.
explanation: Gamora was raised by Thanos, who is her adoptive father. Ronan is a Kree fanatic and an antagonist of the first Guardians film.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Drax the Destroyer was originally a human named Arthur Douglas.
explanation: In the comics Arthur Douglas is killed by Thanos and his spirit is reborn as the Destroyer, Drax.

claim: In the MCU film Guardians of the Galaxy (2014), Drax says his wife and daughter were killed by Thanos.
explanation: In the film Drax blames Ronan the Accuser for killing his family.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Uncle Ben is killed by a burglar whom Peter Parker had earlier chosen not to stop.
explanation: In Spider-Man's origin Peter lets a thief escape, and the same criminal later kills Ben Parker, teaching Peter that great power brings great responsibility.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Spider-Man first appeared in The Amazing Spider-Man #1 (1963).
explanation: Spider-Man debuted in Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962). The Amazing Spider-Man #1 followed in 1963.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Captain America debuted in Captain America Comics #1 (1941), created by Joe Simon and Jack Kirby.
explanation: Captain America Comics #1 was published in 1941 and Simon and Kirby are credited as his creators.

claim: In the MCU film Captain America: The First Avenger, Steve Rogers crashes the Valkyrie plane into the Pacific Ocean.
explanation: Steve crashes the Valkyrie into the Arctic ice, where he is frozen for decades.
source_name: Wikipedia - Captain America: The First Avenger

claim: In the MCU film Iron Man 2, Tony Stark replaces the palladium core of his arc reactor with a new element he synthesizes.
explanation: Palladium in the arc reactor is poisoning Stark, so he creates a new element based on his father's research to replace it.

claim: In the MCU, the Infinity Stone inside Loki's scepter is the Soul Stone.
explanation: The scepter contains the Mind Stone, which is later placed in Vision's forehead in Avengers: Age of Ultron.

claim: In the MCU film Thor: Ragnarok, Mjolnir is destroyed by Hela.
explanation: Hela crushes Mjolnir with her hand, revealing that Thor's power does not depend on the hammer.

claim: In the MCU, Loki is Thor's biological brother, the son of Odin.
explanation: In Thor (2011), Loki learns he is the biological son of Laufey, king of the Frost Giants, and was adopted by Odin.

claim: In the MCU film Avengers: Infinity War, Thor gets his axe Stormbreaker from the dwarf king Eitri on Nidavellir.
explanation: Thor travels to Nidavellir and works with Eitri to forge Stormbreaker in the dying star's forge.

claim: In the MCU, Clint Barton is first introduced in Thor (2011) as an agent of Hydra.
explanation: Clint Barton first appears in Thor (2011) as an agent of S.H.I.E.L.D., not Hydra.

claim: In the MCU, Clint Barton's wife is named Laura.
explanation: Avengers: Age of Ultron introduces Clint's wife Laura Barton and their family on a hidden farm.

claim: In the MCU film The Incredible Hulk (2008), Bruce Banner is hiding in Mexico at the start of the story.
explanation: The film opens with Banner hiding in a favela in Brazil.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Betty Ross is the daughter of General Thaddeus 'Thunderbolt' Ross.
explanation: Betty Ross is Bruce Banner's love interest and the daughter of General Ross, who hunts the Hulk.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Scott Lang was the first Ant-Man.
explanation: Hank Pym was the original Ant-Man. Scott Lang took the identity later, debuting in 1979.

claim: In the MCU film Black Panther, Erik Killmonger's father N'Jobu is the brother of King T'Chaka.
explanation: N'Jobu is T'Chaka's brother, which makes Killmonger T'Challa's cousin.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Doctor Strange's Sanctum Sanctorum is located in Brooklyn Heights.
explanation: The Sanctum Sanctorum is at 177A Bleecker Street in Greenwich Village, Manhattan.

claim: In Marvel Comics, the Punisher's real name is Frank Castle.
explanation: Frank Castle is the vigilante's real name, adopted as the Punisher after his family is killed.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Luke Cage gains his powers through exposure to gamma radiation.
explanation: Luke Cage gets his unbreakable skin and super strength from an experimental procedure in prison, not from gamma radiation.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Marc Spector is empowered as Moon Knight by the Egyptian moon god Khonshu.
explanation: Marc Spector is resurrected as the avatar of Khonshu, the Egyptian god of the moon.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Deadpool's real name is Logan Howlett.
explanation: Deadpool's real name is Wade Wilson. Logan is the name associated with Wolverine.

claim: In the MCU, Thanos collects the Infinity Stones in order to wipe out half of all life in the universe.
explanation: In Avengers: Infinity War, Thanos believes the universe is overpopulated and uses the Infinity Gauntlet to eliminate half of all living beings.

claim: In the MCU, Thanos comes from the planet Xandar.
explanation: Thanos is from Titan, whose collapse he blames on overpopulation. Xandar is the Nova Corps' homeworld.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Thanos is driven to commit atrocities in order to win the love of Death, a cosmic entity personified as a woman.
explanation: In the comics Thanos is obsessed with Mistress Death and carries out mass killings to impress her.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Thanos first appeared in The Avengers #55 (1968).
explanation: Thanos debuted in Iron Man #55 (1973), created by Jim Starlin.

claim: In the MCU film The Avengers (2012), Loki leads an invasion of New York with an army of Chitauri.
explanation: Loki opens a portal over New York and sends the alien Chitauri against Earth, leading to the Battle of New York.

claim: In the MCU film Avengers: Infinity War, Loki is killed by Ebony Maw.
explanation: Loki is killed by Thanos, who strangles him after Loki's failed attempt to stab Thanos.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Norman Osborn is the original Green Goblin.
explanation: Norman Osborn is the first Green Goblin, debuting as a Spider-Man foe in the 1960s. Harry Osborn takes up the identity later.

claim: In Marvel Comics, the Green Goblin first appeared in The Amazing Spider-Man #1 (1963).
explanation: The Green Goblin debuted in The Amazing Spider-Man #14 (1964), not in the first issue.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Gwen Stacy dies in The Amazing Spider-Man #121 (1973) after being thrown from a bridge by the Green Goblin.
explanation: The Night Gwen Stacy Died story in issue #121 shows the Green Goblin throwing her from a bridge, and she dies as Spider-Man tries to save her.

claim: In the MCU film Spider-Man: Homecoming, Peter's classmate Liz Allan is the niece of Adrian Toomes, the Vulture.
explanation: Liz Allan is Adrian Toomes' daughter, not his niece.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Doctor Octopus is Otto Octavius, a scientist whose mechanical arms are fused to his body in a lab accident.
explanation: Otto Octavius's harness of mechanical arms fuses to him during an accident, giving rise to Doctor Octopus.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Kingpin's strength comes from a super-soldier serum.
explanation: Wilson Fisk has no superpowers. He is a peak-human fighter whose strength comes from training and his large frame.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Kingpin first appeared in The Amazing Spider-Man #50 (1967).
explanation: Kingpin debuted as a Spider-Man villain in The Amazing Spider-Man #50, created by Stan Lee and John Romita Sr.

claim: In Marvel Comics, the Venom symbiote bonded with Eddie Brock before it ever bonded with Peter Parker.
explanation: The symbiote first bonded with Peter Parker and became his black costume before it bonded with Eddie Brock.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Eddie Brock is a journalist who blames Spider-Man for ruining his career.
explanation: Brock's career collapses after a story he publishes is discredited, and he blames Spider-Man, which makes him a host for the symbiote.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Carnage's host is Flash Thompson.
explanation: Carnage's host is the serial killer Cletus Kasady. Flash Thompson is the host of Venom as Agent Venom.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Carnage and other symbiotes are vulnerable to fire and loud sound.
explanation: Symbiotes in the comics are established as weak to intense heat and high-frequency sound, which are used to subdue them.

claim: In the MCU film Black Panther, Erik Killmonger helps Ulysses Klaue steal a vibranium artifact from a museum in Paris.
explanation: The artifact is stolen from a museum in London, not Paris.

claim: In the MCU film Black Panther, Killmonger claims the Wakandan throne by defeating T'Challa in ritual combat.
explanation: Killmonger challenges T'Challa under Wakandan tradition, wins the fight and takes the throne.

claim: In the MCU film Guardians of the Galaxy (2014), the Orb that Ronan the Accuser seeks contains the Mind Stone.
explanation: The Orb contains the Power Stone. The Mind Stone is in Loki's scepter.

claim: In the MCU, Ronan the Accuser is a Kree extremist who wants to destroy Xandar.
explanation: Ronan rejects the peace treaty between the Kree and Xandar and plans to destroy the planet using the Power Stone.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Kang the Conqueror is a descendant of Tony Stark.
explanation: Kang is Nathaniel Richards, a descendant of Reed Richards of the Fantastic Four.

claim: In the MCU, He Who Remains, introduced in the Disney+ series Loki, is a variant of Kang the Conqueror.
explanation: He Who Remains is established as a variant of Kang, which sets up the multiverse threat in later MCU stories.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Magneto is the biological father of Cyclops.
explanation: Cyclops (Scott Summers) is the son of Christopher and Katherine Summers. Magneto's children in the comics include Quicksilver and Scarlet Witch.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Magneto is a Holocaust survivor whose birth name is Max Eisenhardt.
explanation: Magneto's comics backstory has him born Max Eisenhardt and surviving the Holocaust, which shapes his views on mutant persecution.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Ultron was created by Tony Stark.
explanation: In the comics Ultron is created by Hank Pym. Tony Stark is the creator only in the MCU, alongside Bruce Banner.

claim: In the MCU film Avengers: Age of Ultron, Ultron is created by Tony Stark and Bruce Banner.
explanation: Stark and Banner secretly build an AI using the Mind Stone's energy, which becomes Ultron.

claim: In the MCU film Captain America: The First Avenger, the Red Skull is killed when Steve Rogers hits him with his shield.
explanation: The Red Skull touches the Tesseract and is disintegrated by it, not killed by the shield.
source_name: Wikipedia - Captain America: The First Avenger

claim: In Marvel Comics, the Red Skull is a Nazi-linked arch-enemy of Captain America.
explanation: The Red Skull is Captain America's best-known adversary, originally an agent of Nazi Germany.

claim: In the MCU film Iron Man (2008), Obadiah Stane is killed by a missile fired by James Rhodes.
explanation: Stane dies when Tony Stark overloads the arc reactor on the roof of Stark Industries and Stane's Iron Monger suit falls into it.

claim: In the MCU film Iron Man 3, the public face of the Mandarin is an actor named Trevor Slattery.
explanation: The film reveals that the Mandarin seen on camera is Trevor Slattery, an actor hired by Aldrich Killian.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Flint Marko becomes the Sandman after being exposed to cosmic rays.
explanation: Marko gains his powers after wandering into a nuclear test site and being exposed to radiation, not cosmic rays.

claim: In the MCU film Spider-Man: Far From Home, Quentin Beck, alias Mysterio, is a former Stark Industries employee.
explanation: Beck is a disgruntled former Stark employee who uses illusion technology to stage fake elemental attacks.

claim: In the MCU film Spider-Man: Homecoming, Adrian Toomes' salvage business is shut down by S.H.I.E.L.D.
explanation: His salvage contract after the Battle of New York is taken over by the Department of Damage Control, which leads him to turn to crime.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Doctor Doom's mother, Cynthia von Doom, made a pact with the demon Mephisto.
explanation: Cynthia von Doom is a sorceress who bargained with Mephisto, and her soul being held by him later drives Doom's attempts to rescue her.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Galactus first appeared in Fantastic Four #1 (1961).
explanation: Galactus debuted in Fantastic Four #48 (1966), as part of the Galactus Trilogy.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Norrin Radd becomes the Silver Surfer by serving as Galactus's herald to save his home planet.
explanation: Norrin Radd agrees to serve Galactus so that the planet Zenn-La will be spared from being consumed.

claim: In Marvel Comics, the mutant Apocalypse was born in ancient Greece.
explanation: Apocalypse, born En Sabah Nur, is established as being born in ancient Egypt thousands of years ago.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Mystique is the mother of Nightcrawler.
explanation: Mystique is Nightcrawler's biological mother; his father is the mutant Azazel.

claim: In Marvel Comics, Bullseye's signature ability is expert archery with a bow.
explanation: Bullseye's signature ability is perfect aim with any thrown object. Archery is Hawkeye's specialty.

claim: In the MCU film The Incredible Hulk (2008), Emil Blonsky is a Royal Marines officer who becomes the Abomination.
explanation: Blonsky, a Russian-born British Royal Marine, takes an enhancement serum and transforms into the Abomination.

claim: In the MCU film Captain America: Civil War, Helmut Zemo is an active agent of Hydra.
explanation: Zemo is a Sokovian former military officer driven by revenge for his family's death, not a Hydra agent.

claim: In the MCU film Doctor Strange (2016), Stephen Strange defeats Dormammu by trapping him in a time loop.
explanation: Strange uses the Eye of Agamotto to loop time and repeatedly dies until Dormammu agrees to leave Earth alone.

claim: In the MCU film Doctor Strange (2016), Kaecilius is a former student of Baron Mordo.
explanation: Kaecilius is a former student of the Ancient One who breaks away after turning to Dormammu's power.

claim: In the MCU film Black Panther: Wakanda Forever, Namor rules the underwater kingdom of Talokan.
explanation: Namor is the leader of the Talokanil, an underwater civilization, and becomes an antagonist to Wakanda.

claim: In the MCU, Hela is Thor's younger sister.
explanation: In Thor: Ragnarok, Hela is Odin's firstborn child, making her Thor's older sister.

claim: In the MCU film Thor: The Dark World, Malekith, the leader of the Dark Elves, seeks the Aether.
explanation: Malekith wants to use the Aether to plunge the universe into darkness during the Convergence.

claim: In the MCU, the Aether from Thor: The Dark World is later revealed to be the Space Stone.
explanation: The Aether is the Reality Stone. The Space Stone is the Tesseract.

claim: In the MCU film Avengers: Infinity War, the Red Skull appears as the keeper of the Soul Stone on Vormir.
explanation: The Red Skull is revealed as Stonekeeper on Vormir, guiding those who seek the Soul Stone.

claim: In the MCU film Avengers: Infinity War, Thanos obtains the Soul Stone by sacrificing Nebula.
explanation: Thanos sacrifices Gamora to obtain the Soul Stone.

claim: MCU: The Mind Stone was embedded in Vision's forehead.
explanation: The Mind Stone powers Vision's body after Ultron's creation in Avengers: Age of Ultron and remains in his forehead until Thanos removes it in Infinity War.

claim: MCU: The Soul Stone was found on the planet Xandar.
explanation: The Soul Stone was on Vormir. Xandar is the Nova Corps homeworld where the Power Stone was stored after Guardians of the Galaxy.

claim: MCU: Thor's axe Stormbreaker was forged on Nidavellir.
explanation: In Infinity War, Thor, Rocket and Groot travel to Nidavellir, where the dwarf king Eitri forges Stormbreaker.

claim: MCU: Thanos destroyed Mjolnir in Avengers: Infinity War.
explanation: Mjolnir was destroyed by Hela in Thor: Ragnarok, not by Thanos.

claim: MCU: Pym Particles shrink objects by reducing the distance between atoms.
explanation: In Ant-Man, Hank Pym explains that his particles reduce the space between atoms, shrinking size while keeping mass.

claim: MCU: Scott Lang discovered Pym Particles.
explanation: Hank Pym discovered Pym Particles. Scott Lang only inherits the Ant-Man suit and technology.

claim: Comics: Hank Pym created Ultron.
explanation: In the comics, Ultron was created by Hank Pym, who is also the original Ant-Man.

claim: MCU: Ultron was created by Tony Stark and Hank Pym.
explanation: In the MCU, Ultron is created by Tony Stark and Bruce Banner in Age of Ultron. Hank Pym is not involved.

claim: Comics: The 1991 Infinity Gauntlet series was written by Jim Starlin.
explanation: The Infinity Gauntlet (1991) was written by Jim Starlin and illustrated by George Pérez and Ron Lim.

claim: Comics: In the 1991 Infinity Gauntlet, Thanos acted mainly to end overpopulation.
explanation: In the 1991 comic, Thanos's motive is to win the affection of the entity Death. The overpopulation motive belongs to the MCU.

claim: Comics (Earth-616): Mjolnir is forged from the metal Uru.
explanation: In mainstream Marvel comics, Mjolnir was forged from Uru, an enchantable Asgardian metal.

claim: MCU: Thor lost his eye during the Battle of New York.
explanation: Thor loses his eye in a fight with Hela in Thor: Ragnarok, not in The Avengers (2012).

claim: MCU: The Hulkbuster armor is Iron Man's Mark 44.
explanation: In Age of Ultron, the Hulkbuster is the Mark 44 armor, built to contain Hulk.

claim: MCU: Tony Stark's new arc reactor core in Iron Man 2 was based on vibranium.
explanation: Tony synthesizes a new element, using a design from Howard Stark's research. Vibranium is not used in Iron Man 2.

claim: MCU: The Black Panther gains his powers from the Heart-Shaped Herb.
explanation: In Black Panther, the herb grants T'Challa enhanced strength, speed and senses.

claim: MCU: Wakanda is located in South America.
explanation: Wakanda is a fictional nation in Africa.

claim: MCU: The Time Stone is housed in the Eye of Agamotto.
explanation: Doctor Strange wears the Eye of Agamotto, which contains the Time Stone.

claim: MCU: Thanos took the Time Stone from Doctor Strange by force on Titan.
explanation: Strange willingly gives Thanos the Time Stone to save Tony Stark's life.

claim: MCU: In Endgame, Bruce Banner persuades the Ancient One to give up the Time Stone.
explanation: Banner meets the Ancient One in 2012 New York and convinces her to hand over the Time Stone, which she lends on the condition that it is returned.

claim: MCU: The Battle of New York took place in 2018.
explanation: The Battle of New York takes place in 2012 in The Avengers.

claim: Comics: The Fantastic Four gained powers from cosmic rays during a space flight.
explanation: Reed Richards, Sue Storm, Johnny Storm and Ben Grimm are exposed to cosmic rays on an experimental rocket flight.

claim: Comics: Johnny Storm is the Fantastic Four's rock-skinned Thing.
explanation: The Thing is Ben Grimm. Johnny Storm is the Human Torch.

claim: MCU: Peter Quill's father, Ego, is a Celestial.
explanation: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 reveals Ego as a Celestial who created a living planet around himself.
source_name: Wikipedia: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2

claim: MCU: Nebula is Thanos's biological daughter.
explanation: Thanos adopted Nebula and Gamora. Neither is his biological child.

claim: Comics: Professor X uses Cerebro to detect mutants.
explanation: Cerebro is a device that amplifies Charles Xavier's telepathy to locate mutants.

claim: Comics: Storm was a founding member of the original 1963 X-Men.
explanation: Storm debuted in Giant-Size X-Men #1 (1975) as part of the new X-Men team.

claim: Comics: Sentinels are giant robots built to hunt mutants.
explanation: Sentinels are mutant-hunting robots in the X-Men comics.

claim: Comics: Wolverine's skeleton is bonded with vibranium.
explanation: Wolverine's skeleton and claws are bonded with adamantium, not vibranium.

claim: Comics: Thanos is an Eternal from the moon Titan.
explanation: In the comics, Thanos is the son of A'Lars and a member of the Titan branch of the Eternals.

claim: Comics: Doctor Doom rules the nation of Wakanda.
explanation: Doctor Doom rules Latveria. Wakanda is the home of the Black Panther.

claim: Comics: The Silver Surfer was a herald of Galactus.
explanation: Norrin Radd becomes the Silver Surfer to serve as Galactus's herald and spare his homeworld.

claim: Comics: Galactus was born in the same universe he now devours.
explanation: Galactus began as Galan of Taa in the universe that preceded the current one.

claim: MCU: Bruce Banner was the first Avenger to use the Nano Gauntlet to reverse the Blip.
explanation: In Endgame, Banner snaps with the Nano Gauntlet and restores those who vanished.

claim: MCU: Tony Stark wielded Mjolnir in Avengers: Endgame.
explanation: Captain America wields Mjolnir in Endgame. Tony Stark does not.

claim: MCU: Rocket Raccoon was created by the High Evolutionary.
explanation: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 shows the High Evolutionary experimenting on Rocket.
source_name: Wikipedia: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3

claim: MCU: Ronan the Accuser sought the Mind Stone in Guardians of the Galaxy.
explanation: Ronan sought the Power Stone, held in the Orb. The Mind Stone was elsewhere.

claim: MCU: The Sokovia Accords are named after the country devastated in Age of Ultron.
explanation: The Accords are named for Sokovia, where the Avengers fought Ultron, and they regulate enhanced individuals.

claim: MCU: The Guardians of the Galaxy first meet in the Knowhere prison.
explanation: They meet in the Kyln, a Nova Corps prison. Knowhere is a different location.

claim: MCU: The Time Variance Authority prunes variant timelines.
explanation: In the Loki series, the TVA removes timelines that branch away from the Sacred Timeline.

claim: MCU: Scott Lang was the first person to enter the Quantum Realm.
explanation: Janet van Dyne became trapped in the Quantum Realm in 1987, long before Scott Lang.

claim: Comics: The first Cosmic Cube was created by A.I.M.
explanation: The first Cosmic Cube was built by the scientific organization Advanced Idea Mechanics (A.I.M.).

claim: Comics: Captain America was a founding member of the Avengers.
explanation: Cap joined in Avengers #4. The founders were Iron Man, Thor, Ant-Man, the Wasp and Hulk.

claim: MCU: In Endgame, Banner says changing the past creates branched timelines.
explanation: Banner explains that altering the past does not change the Avengers' own present, but creates a branch reality.

claim: MCU: Obadiah Stane helped Tony Stark build the Mark I armor in captivity.
explanation: Ho Yinsen helped Tony build the Mark I. Stane is Tony's betrayer.

claim: Comics: Vibranium absorbs vibrations and kinetic energy.
explanation: Marvel's vibranium is a fictional metal that absorbs vibrations and kinetic energy.

claim: MCU: Thanos's snap erased 10% of all life in the universe.
explanation: The snap erases half of all life in the universe.

claim: MCU: Vision lifted Mjolnir in Avengers: Age of Ultron.
explanation: Vision lifts Mjolnir and hands it to Thor, demonstrating that he is worthy.

claim: Comics: Magneto is Professor X's biological brother.
explanation: Magneto and Xavier are friends turned adversaries, not brothers.

claim: MCU: Groot belongs to the Flora colossus species.
explanation: Groot is a Flora colossus, a tree-like extraterrestrial species.

claim: MCU: Thanos is from the planet Xandar.
explanation: Thanos is from Titan. Xandar is the Nova Corps homeworld.

claim: Comics: Spider-Man first appeared in Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962).
explanation: Peter Parker debuted in Amazing Fantasy #15, created by Stan Lee and Steve Ditko, before getting his own series.

claim: Comics: The Hulk's skin was green in The Incredible Hulk #1 (1962).
explanation: The Hulk was gray in his first issue. His color was changed to green starting with issue #2 because of printing problems.

claim: Comics: Kamala Khan, the modern Ms. Marvel, is from Jersey City.
explanation: Kamala Khan is a Pakistani-American teenager living in Jersey City, New Jersey.

claim: Comics: Carol Danvers was the first hero to use the name Captain Marvel.
explanation: Mar-Vell, a Kree warrior, was the first Marvel Comics Captain Marvel. Carol Danvers took the name later.

claim: Comics: Daredevil's heightened senses came from exposure to radioactive material.
explanation: Matt Murdock was blinded by a radioactive substance, which sharpened his remaining senses.

claim: Comics: Daredevil's secret identity is Foggy Nelson.
explanation: Daredevil is Matt Murdock. Foggy Nelson is his best friend and law partner.

claim: Comics: Stephen Strange was a neurosurgeon before becoming a sorcerer.
explanation: Strange was a renowned surgeon whose hands were damaged in a car accident, which led him to seek mystical healing.

claim: Comics: Doctor Strange first trained under the Ancient One in Egypt.
explanation: In the comics, Strange travels to the Himalayas in Tibet to find the Ancient One. The MCU film changes the location to Kamar-Taj in Nepal.

claim: Comics: Moon Knight's powers are granted by the Egyptian moon god Khonshu.
explanation: Marc Spector, a mercenary, is revived by Khonshu and becomes the god's avatar.

claim: Comics: Johnny Blaze made his Ghost Rider deal with Dormammu.
explanation: Johnny Blaze sold his soul to Mephisto, not Dormammu.

claim: Comics: Blade debuted in The Tomb of Dracula #10 (1973).
explanation: Blade was created by Marv Wolfman and Gene Colan and first appeared in The Tomb of Dracula #10, not in a film.

claim: Comics: Wolverine's birth name is Logan.
explanation: Wolverine was born James Howlett. Logan is the name he adopted.

claim: MCU: Wanda and Pietro Maximoff are twins.
explanation: In Avengers: Age of Ultron, Wanda and Pietro are twin siblings from Sokovia.

claim: MCU: Loki is Odin's biological son.
explanation: In Thor (2011), Loki learns he is the biological son of Laufey, king of the Frost Giants, and was adopted by Odin.

claim: Comics: Hela is the daughter of Loki.
explanation: In the comics, Hela is Loki's daughter with Angrboda. This differs from the MCU, where she is Odin's daughter.

claim: Comics: Peter Parker was bitten by a radioactive spider at Oscorp.
explanation: In the original comics, Peter is bitten at a science exhibition. Oscorp's role comes from later adaptations.

claim: Comics: Ultron built Vision using the body of the original Human Torch.
explanation: In Avengers #134-135, Ultron creates Vision from the android body of the original Human Torch. Vision later turns against Ultron.

claim: Comics: Hawkeye gained his skills from a super-soldier serum.
explanation: Clint Barton has no superpowers. He is a master archer trained through years of practice.

claim: Comics: In House of M, Scarlet Witch declares 'No more mutants.'
explanation: After the reality-altering events of House of M, Wanda's words strip the powers from most of the world's mutants.

claim: Comics: Black Widow debuted in Tales of Suspense #39.
explanation: Black Widow debuted in Tales of Suspense #52 (1964). Issue #39 is Iron Man's debut.

claim: Comics: Black Panther debuted in Fantastic Four #52 (1966).
explanation: T'Challa first appeared in Fantastic Four #52, created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby.

claim: Comics: Thor's first mortal alter ego, Donald Blake, was a veterinarian.
explanation: Donald Blake was a physician, not a veterinarian.

claim: Comics: Captain America Comics #1 (1941) shows Cap punching Hitler on its cover.
explanation: The cover of Captain America Comics #1, by Joe Simon and Jack Kirby, shows Cap hitting Adolf Hitler.

claim: Comics: Cyclops's younger brother is Quicksilver.
explanation: Cyclops's younger brother is Alex Summers, also known as Havok. Quicksilver is Pietro Maximoff.

claim: Comics: Miles Morales originated in the Ultimate Marvel universe, Earth-1610.
explanation: Miles Morales debuted in the Ultimate Marvel imprint (Earth-1610) before later joining the main continuity.

claim: Comics: The Dark Phoenix Saga was written by Stan Lee.
explanation: The Dark Phoenix Saga was written by Chris Claremont and illustrated by John Byrne.

claim: Comics: Iron Man debuted in Tales of Suspense #39 (1963).
explanation: Tony Stark's Iron Man first appeared in Tales of Suspense #39, in a story by Stan Lee and Larry Lieber.

claim: Comics: The Kree and Skrull empires are long-time allies.
explanation: The Kree and Skrulls are enemies, most famously in the Kree-Skrull War.

claim: Comics: Rocket Raccoon debuted in Marvel Preview #7 (1976).
explanation: Rocket Raccoon first appeared in Marvel Preview #7, years before his Guardians of the Galaxy fame.

claim: MCU: Namor rules the underwater kingdom of Atlantis.
explanation: In Black Panther: Wakanda Forever, Namor rules Talokan. Atlantis is his kingdom in the comics.

claim: Comics: Wolverine first appeared in The Incredible Hulk #180-181 (1974).
explanation: Wolverine debuted in the Hulk's own series before joining the X-Men.

claim: Comics: Miles Morales is a clone of Peter Parker.
explanation: Miles is an independent teenager bitten by a genetically altered spider. The clone is Ben Reilly.

claim: Comics: Deadpool debuted in The New Mutants #98 (1991).
explanation: Deadpool was created by Rob Liefeld and Fabian Nicieza and first appeared in The New Mutants #98.

claim: Comics: The Wasp, Janet van Dyne, is Hank Pym's sister.
explanation: Janet van Dyne is Hank Pym's wife and a founding Avenger.

claim: Comics: The Eternals were created by Jack Kirby in 1976.
explanation: Kirby created the Eternals for Marvel in 1976, building on his ideas about ancient cosmic beings.

claim: Comics: Nick Fury first appeared in Avengers #1 (1963).
explanation: Nick Fury debuted in Sgt. Fury and His Howling Commandos #1 (1963) as a WWII soldier. His modern spy version appeared in Fantastic Four #21.

claim: Comics: S.H.I.E.L.D. originally stood for Supreme Headquarters, International Espionage, Law-Enforcement Division.
explanation: This was the original name in the comics. It was later changed to Strategic Homeland Intervention, Enforcement and Logistics Division.

claim: Comics: Rocket Raccoon is a natural Earth raccoon.
explanation: Rocket is from the planet Halfworld, where he was engineered and not an Earth animal.

claim: Comics: Hydra's motto is 'Cut off one limb, two more shall take its place.'
explanation: This is Hydra's well-known slogan, referencing the many-headed serpent from Greek myth.

claim: Comics: Doctor Strange's Sanctum Sanctorum is located in Brooklyn.
explanation: The Sanctum Sanctorum is on Bleecker Street in Greenwich Village, Manhattan.

claim: Comics: Dormammu rules the Dark Dimension.
explanation: Dormammu is the ruler of the Dark Dimension and one of Doctor Strange's greatest enemies.

claim: Comics: The Inhumans originated from the Skrull Empire.
explanation: The Inhumans were created through Kree genetic experiments on early humans, not by the Skrulls.

claim: Comics: Adam Warlock was first created by the Enclave under the name Him.
explanation: Scientists called the Enclave created the artificial being Him, who later became Adam Warlock.

claim: Comics: Vision is a mutant.
explanation: Vision is a synthezoid, an artificial android, not a mutant.

claim: Comics: Hawkeye first appeared as a villain in an Iron Man story.
explanation: Hawkeye debuted in Tales of Suspense #57 as an antagonist to Iron Man, then later joined the Avengers.

claim: Comics: The Punisher debuted in Daredevil #1.
explanation: The Punisher debuted in The Amazing Spider-Man #129 (1974) as a Spider-Man antagonist.

claim: Comics: Namor first appeared in Marvel Comics #1 (1939).
explanation: Namor the Sub-Mariner was one of Marvel's earliest characters, debuting in Marvel Comics #1 in 1939.

claim: Comics: Angel (Warren Worthington III) comes from a poor family.
explanation: Warren Worthington III is the heir to a wealthy family fortune.

claim: MCU: Steve Rogers hands Sam Wilson the Captain America shield in Endgame.
explanation: In Avengers: Endgame, an elderly Steve Rogers gives Sam the shield and passes on the mantle.

claim: Comics: Nightcrawler's biological mother is Rogue.
explanation: Nightcrawler's biological mother is Mystique. Rogue is Mystique's adopted daughter.
